Edmund, Edg. Edgar, Gon. Goneril, Reg. Regan, Cor. Cordelia, Alb. Albany, Osw. Oswald, Gent. Gentleman, Doct. Doctor, Mess. Messenger, Capt. Captain, Her. Herald). Trill'd means trickled; smilets, little smiles; one self mate and mate, one and the same husband and wife; elbows, jostles; casualties, chances; fumiter, furrow-weeds, bur-docks, hemlock, cuckoo-flowers and darnel are weeds of the fields; a century is a company of a hundred soldiers; simples are healing herbs; aidant and remediate, helpful and healing; important, pleading; blown, puffed up; œillades, amorous glances; of her bosom, in her confidence; nighted, darkened; descry, discover; preferment, promotion.

excerpt.locator: King Lear, Act IV, scenes III to V; opens “Enter Kent and a Gentleman.”; closes “Reg. Fare thee well. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: The Gentleman describes Cordelia reading the letters as “a queen Over her passion.” How does his description shape your idea of her before she appears?
facilitatorNotes: Her grief is strong but governed: “patience and sorrow strove,” smiles and tears come together, and when she breaks out she leaves “To deal with grief alone.” The pictures of sunshine and rain and of pearls dropping from diamonds make her almost a painting. Some readers find the language too ornate, a saint’s portrait; others find it true to the daughter who in Act I would not perform her love in words.
evidence: it seem'd she was a queen Over her passion, who most rebel-like Sought to be king o'er her.
Sunshine and rain at once:
To deal with grief alone.

questions.prompt: Kent says “It is the stars... govern our conditions.” What is he trying to explain, and does the rest of his talk with the Gentleman support it?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot see how the same parents could make Cordelia and her sisters, so he blames the stars, the view Edmund mocked in Act I. Yet when he explains why Lear will not see Cordelia, he gives a human cause, “A sovereign shame.” The scene invokes fate and then shows character at work; students may decide which explanation the play trusts.
evidence: It is the stars, The stars above us, govern our conditions;
A sovereign shame so elbows him:
burning shame Detains him from Cordelia.

questions.prompt: Cordelia insists “No blown ambition doth our arms incite.” Why does she need to say this, and who might doubt her?
facilitatorNotes: She leads a French army into Britain; to the British it is an invasion, as Albany will say. She claims a private motive, “love, dear love, and our aged father's right,” and now says aloud the love she would not declare in Act I. Her list of weeds in Lear’s crown, “idle weeds” growing in “sustaining corn,” pictures his mind overgrown yet still among things that feed.
evidence: No blown ambition doth our arms incite, But love, dear love, and our aged father's right:
It is thy business that I go about;
Darnel, and all the idle weeds that grow In our sustaining corn.

questions.prompt: In scene V Regan questions Oswald about a letter. What does she want, how does she try to get it, and what does the scene reveal?
facilitatorNotes: She wants to read Goneril’s letter to Edmund; she flatters (“I'll love thee much”), then tells Oswald she is a widow and so more “convenient” for Edmund. The sisters are now rivals. She also regrets letting Gloucester live and sets a price on him. Oswald’s refusal shows a servant loyal to his mistress’s vices, as the play will call him.
evidence: Let me unseal the letter.
And more convenient is he for my hand Than for your lady's:
It was great ignorance, Gloucester's eyes being out, To let him live:
Preferment falls on him that cuts him off.

readings.title: King Lear — the cliff at Dover (IV.6)
readings.challenge: Read the scene twice: once as Gloucester lives it, once as Edgar stages it.
readings.focus: A son who saves his father from suicide by deceiving him.
readings.context: Recap: Edgar, disguised as the mad beggar Poor Tom, promised to lead his blinded father to the brink of a cliff at Dover, where Gloucester means to end his life; Gloucester still does not know who his guide is. Cordelia has landed at Dover with a French army, and the mad Lear wanders near her camp. Regan has promised a reward to whoever kills Gloucester. Edgar has now changed into a peasant’s clothes. King Lear, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Glou. Gloucester, Edm. Edmund, Edg. Edgar, Gon. Goneril, Reg. Regan, Cor. Cordelia, Alb. Albany, Osw. Oswald, Gent. Gentleman, Doct. Doctor, Mess. Messenger, Capt. Captain, Her. Herald). Choughs are jackdaws; samphire is a cliff plant gathered for pickling; a bark is a ship and her cock its small boat; the snuff is the burnt end of a candle wick; conceit means imagination; bourn, boundary; a-height, on high; whelk'd, twisted; the clearest gods, the purest and most glorious.
readings.contentNote: Gloucester attempts suicide; the fall is staged, but his despair is real.

excerpt.locator: King Lear, Act IV, scene VI, from the opening to Edgar’s “Bear free and patient thoughts”; opens “Enter Gloucester, and Edgar dressed like a peasant.”; closes “Edg. Bear free and patient thoughts. But who comes here?”.

questions.prompt: Gloucester notices that the ground is even and that his guide’s voice has changed. How does Edgar meet these doubts, and what does the exchange do for an audience?
facilitatorNotes: He contradicts each one: the ground is “Horrible steep,” Gloucester’s other senses are failing, and he is changed only “in my garments,” which is true in a way, since he is Edgar underneath. On a bare stage the audience sees no cliff either, so the play makes us aware of the illusion at the very moment it builds one.
evidence: Methinks the ground is even.
Horrible steep.
You're much deceived: in nothing am I changed But in my garments.

questions.prompt: How does Edgar make the height felt with words alone? Look at the sizes he gives things and at how his speech ends.
facilitatorNotes: Everything shrinks in sequence: birds to beetles, the samphire gatherer to the size of his head, fishermen to mice, a ship to its small boat and the boat to a buoy; even the surf cannot be heard. The eye travels down and out, and the speech ends in vertigo. The description is so convincing that readers half believe the cliff themselves.
evidence: The crows and choughs that wing the midway air Show scarce so gross as beetles:
Appear like mice;
Lest my brain turn and the deficient sight Topple down headlong.

questions.prompt: Edgar says, “Why I do trifle thus with his despair Is done to cure it.” Is his trick kind, cruel, or both?
facilitatorNotes: He means to persuade his father that the gods saved him (“Thy life's a miracle”) so that he will choose to live, and it works: Gloucester vows to bear affliction. But it is a deception practised on a man at prayer, and it delays the truth Gloucester most needs, who his guide is. Some readers admire the care; others find Edgar theatrical, even controlling.
evidence: Why I do trifle thus with his despair Is done to cure it.
Thy life's a miracle.
henceforth I'll bear Affliction till it do cry out itself 'Enough, enough,' and die.

questions.prompt: How has Gloucester’s idea of the gods changed between his prayer before the fall and his last speech here? What is it built on?
facilitatorNotes: Before the fall he would end his life rather than “quarrel” with wills he cannot oppose. Afterwards he accepts that the “clearest gods” preserved him and that the urge to die came from a fiend. Endurance replaces despair, but the fiend is Edgar’s invention. Students can ask whether a faith reached through a fiction is less true, or whether the fiction only made room for a truth.
evidence: To quarrel with your great opposeless wills,
Think that the clearest gods, who make them honours Of men's impossibilities, have preserved thee.
'The fiend, the fiend:' he led me to that place.

readings.title: King Lear — “Reason in madness” (IV.6)
readings.challenge: Follow Lear’s mad talk for its hidden argument: find what he says about power, justice and seeing.
readings.focus: The mad king and the blind earl meet, and see the world more clearly than before.
readings.context: Recap: Edgar, in disguise, has led his blinded father to what he said was the edge of the Dover cliff; Gloucester leapt, fell only to the ground, was persuaded that the gods saved him, and has resolved to bear his suffering. He still does not know his guide. Lear has escaped from the people Cordelia sent to find him and wanders crowned with wild flowers. King Lear, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Glou. Gloucester, Edm. Edmund, Edg. Edgar, Gon. Goneril, Reg. Regan, Cor. Cordelia, Alb. Albany, Osw. Oswald, Gent. Gentleman, Doct. Doctor, Mess. Messenger, Capt. Captain, Her. Herald). Coining means making money, a king’s right; press-money, a recruit’s pay; a crow-keeper, a scarecrow; a clothier's yard, the length of an arrow; brown bills, soldiers’ halberds; the clout, the centre of a target; the word, a password; luxury, lust; a fitchew is a polecat and a soiled horse one fed on fresh grass; civet, a perfume; squiny, squint; handy-dandy, a children’s game of guessing which hand holds something; a beadle, a parish officer who whipped offenders; a cozener, a cheat; able, vouch for; a politician, a schemer; a block may be a hat or a mounting-block; a man of salt, all tears; smug, spruce; descry, sight; pregnant, ready; benison, blessing.
readings.contentNote: Lear’s madness turns to disgust at sex and at women’s bodies, and ends in a cry to kill; he speaks of a woman whipped as a whore.

excerpt.locator: King Lear, Act IV, scene VI, from Lear’s entrance to Edgar’s offer to lead Gloucester to shelter; opens “Enter Lear, fantastically dressed with wild flowers.”; closes “Glou. Hearty thanks: The bounty and the benison of heaven To boot, and boot!”.

questions.prompt: “Ay, every inch a king”: what does Lear do with his kingship in the lines that follow? Is he more or less a king here than in Act I?
facilitatorNotes: He pardons an imaginary adulterer, reasoning that Gloucester’s bastard son was kinder to his father than Lear’s lawful daughters were to him, and plays judge and recruiting captain. His power is imaginary, but his judgement is sharper than when he ruled. The line can be played as pathos, a man in weeds claiming a crown, or as a truth: he is at last a king in insight.
evidence: Ay, every inch a king:
for Gloucester's bastard son Was kinder to his father than my daughters Got 'tween the lawful sheets.

questions.prompt: What did the storm teach Lear about the people who flattered him and about himself?
facilitatorNotes: The flatterers agreed with everything; the rain and thunder would not obey him, and that showed him the lie. He is “not ague-proof”: a king’s body catches cold like anyone’s. When Gloucester asks to kiss his hand, Lear wipes it because it “smells of mortality.” Royalty no longer hides the body.
evidence: They flattered me like a dog,
they told me I was every thing; 'tis a lie, I am not ague-proof.
Let me wipe it first; it smells of mortality.

questions.prompt: “A man may see how this world goes with no eyes.” What does Lear teach the blind Gloucester about justice? Is his argument mad?
facilitatorNotes: Judge and thief could change places without anyone telling them apart; a dog in office is obeyed; the beadle lusts after the woman he whips; rags show small sins while robes hide great ones; if all are guilty, “None does offend.” Gloucester answers that he sees it “feelingly,” through suffering. The argument is sane and even radical; Edgar names the paradox: “Reason in madness!”
evidence: change places, and, handy-dandy, which is the justice, which is the thief?
Through tatter'd clothes small vices do appear; Robes and furr'd gowns hide all.
I see it feelingly.
O, matter and impertinency mix'd! Reason in madness!

questions.prompt: Lear preaches that “we came crying hither,” then imagines killing his sons-in-law and runs from Cordelia’s men. What does the turn tell you about his state, and what does the Gentleman add?
facilitatorNotes: The sermon is wise: birth is crying at entering “this great stage of fools.” But patience gives way at once to revenge, and when rescue comes he thinks himself taken prisoner, “The natural fool of fortune.” He cannot yet receive help. The Gentleman’s line about the one daughter who “redeems nature” prepares the reunion the audience is waiting for.
evidence: Thou must be patient; we came crying hither:
When we are born, we cry that we are come To this great stage of fools.
I am even The natural fool of fortune.
Thou hast one daughter, Who redeems nature from the general curse Which twain have brought her to.

readings.title: King Lear — “a very foolish fond old man” (IV.6–7)
readings.challenge: Notice how each person in these scenes is recognised, or fails to be: by voice, by letter, by face.
readings.focus: A servant’s death, a plot exposed, and a father and daughter reunited.
readings.context: Recap: At Dover the mad Lear met the blinded Gloucester and preached to him about justice before running from the people Cordelia sent to find him. Edgar, still unknown to his father, has offered to lead Gloucester to shelter. Regan gave Oswald, Goneril’s steward, a message for Edmund and promised a reward to whoever kills Gloucester. King Lear, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Glou. Gloucester, Edm. Edmund, Edg. Edgar, Gon. Goneril, Reg. Regan, Cor. Cordelia, Alb. Albany, Osw. Oswald, Gent. Gentleman, Doct. Doctor, Mess. Messenger, Capt. Captain, Her. Herald). Edgar puts on the speech of a West Country peasant: chill and chud are I will and I would; che vor ye, I warn you; zwaggered, bullied; costard, head; ballow, cudgel; foins, thrusts. A deathsman is an executioner; gentle wax, the letter’s seal; undistinguish'd space, boundless reach; rake up, bury; the death-practised duke, Albany, whose death is plotted; ingenious, conscious; distract, mad. Scene VII opens, as its heading sets it, with Lear asleep on a bed while soft music plays. Weeds are clothes; made intent, plan; child-changed, changed by his children; a perdu, a sentry in the most exposed post; fond, foolish; even o'er, piece together; arbitrement, decision; point and period, aim and end.
readings.contentNote: Edgar kills Oswald in a fight; Goneril’s letter invites her lover to murder her husband.

excerpt.locator: King Lear, Act IV, from Oswald’s entrance in scene VI to the end of scene VII; opens “Enter Oswald.”; closes “…period will be throughly wrought, Or well or ill, as this day's battle's fought. [Exit.”.

questions.prompt: When Oswald comes to kill Gloucester, Edgar speaks as a peasant. What does the fight show about Oswald, and what is Edgar’s verdict on him?
facilitatorNotes: Oswald sneers at the “bold peasant” and “dunghill” and is beaten by a man with a cudgel. Dying, he asks his killer to bury him and to deliver his mistress’s letters: loyal to the end, to a bad cause. Edgar’s epitaph, “a serviceable villain,” sums up a servant who did whatever he was told. Students might ask whether that loyalty earns any pity.
evidence: Wherefore, bold peasant, Darest thou support a publish'd traitor?
Chill pick your teeth, zir:
a serviceable villain, As duteous to the vices of thy mistress As badness would desire.

questions.prompt: What does Goneril’s letter ask of Edmund, and what does Edgar mean to do with it?
facilitatorNotes: She reminds Edmund of their vows and asks him to kill Albany (“cut him off”) and take his place; she signs herself his “wife, so I would say.” Edgar buries Oswald and keeps the letter to show Albany “in the mature time.” The paper becomes the evidence that brings Edmund down in Act V.
evidence: You have many opportunities to cut him off:
'Your—wife, so I would say—affectionate servant,
With this ungracious paper strike the sight Of the death-practised duke:

questions.prompt: Gloucester envies the king his madness. Why, and do the scenes you have read support him?
facilitatorNotes: Madness would sever “my thoughts... from my griefs”; sanity keeps him upright and aware of every sorrow. Yet Lear’s madness has not freed him from pain: he called himself “cut to the brains,” and waking he is bound “Upon a wheel of fire.” Some readers find Gloucester’s wish understandable; others think the play shows no escape either way.
evidence: Better I were distract: So should my thoughts be sever'd from my griefs,
how stiff is my vile sense, That I stand up, and have ingenious feeling Of my huge sorrows!

questions.prompt: Trace the steps by which Lear wakes to recognise Cordelia. What does each step show, and what is her answer to his guilt?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks himself dragged from the grave and her a soul in bliss; he doubts his own hands; he admits he is “a very foolish fond old man” before he dares name “my child Cordelia.” He expects poison because she has “some cause.” Her “No cause, no cause” forgives without argument, as her “Nothing” in Act I refused to argue for love. He kneels and she forbids it; he ends asking to “forget and forgive.”
evidence: You do me wrong to take me out o' the grave:
I am a very foolish fond old man,
You have some cause, they have not.
No cause, no cause.
Pray you now, forget and forgive: I am old and foolish.

readings.title: King Lear — “Ripeness is all” (V.1–3)
readings.challenge: Notice which speeches are made in public and which aside, and what each speaker hides.
readings.focus: Two sisters jealous over one man, a battle fought in a stage direction, and a king who wants only a prison with his daughter.
readings.context: This run begins Act V of King Lear, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Glou. Gloucester, Edm. Edmund, Edg. Edgar, Gon. Goneril, Reg. Regan, Cor. Cordelia, Alb. Albany, Osw. Oswald, Gent. Gentleman, Doct. Doctor, Mess. Messenger, Capt. Captain, Her. Herald). Recap: Lear, mad, was found near Dover by Cordelia’s people; he woke to music in her tent and knew her, asking her to forget and forgive. Edgar, still in disguise, has killed Goneril’s steward Oswald and found on him Goneril’s letter urging Edmund to murder her husband, Albany. Regan, now Cornwall’s widow, wants Edmund for herself. Edmund leads the British forces against the French army that Cordelia brought. Conjunct and bosom'd mean joined and intimate; forfended, forbidden; be-met, met; bolds, encourages; the ancient of war, the experienced officers; avouched, asserted; o'erlook, read over; taking off, killing; to censure is to judge; God's spies are watchers sent by God; packs and sects, factions; a brand, a torch; foxes were smoked out of their holes; the good-years, some evil power; fell, skin.

excerpt.locator: King Lear, Act V, scenes I and II and the opening of scene III, to Lear and Cordelia led away to prison; opens “Enter, with drum and colours, Edmund, Regan, Gentlemen, and Soldiers.”; closes “…shall make us weep: we'll see 'em starve first. Come. [Exeunt Lear and Cordelia, guarded.”.

questions.prompt: “Which of them shall I take? Both? one? or neither?” What does Edmund’s soliloquy show about how he sees the sisters, Albany and the prisoners?
facilitatorNotes: People are pieces in a game: each sister is jealous “as the stung Are of the adder,” Albany is useful for the battle and then Goneril can kill him, and the mercy Albany intends for Lear and Cordelia will never be carried out. His last line makes his own position the only value. The soliloquy prepares the order he will give in the next scene.
evidence: To both these sisters have I sworn my love;
Let her who would be rid of him devise His speedy taking off.
Shall never see his pardon; for my state Stands on me to defend, not to debate.

questions.prompt: Albany says he fights because France invades, not to oppose the king. Why does he draw this line, and what does it say about his position?
facilitatorNotes: He will defend the country but admits that Lear and others have “just and heavy causes” for opposing them; he is honest about the dilemma (“Where I could not be honest, I never yet was valiant”). It is the stance of a decent man on the wrong side. Regan’s “Why is this reason'd?” shows how little patience the others have for scruple.
evidence: It toucheth us, as France invades our land, Not bolds the king,
Where I could not be honest, I never yet was valiant:
Why is this reason'd?

questions.prompt: The battle passes in a stage direction between two short speeches of Edgar’s. Why might the play give it so little space? What does “Ripeness is all” answer?
facilitatorNotes: The play cares about the result, “King Lear hath lost,” not the fighting. Gloucester falls back into despair, “a man may rot even here,” and Edgar answers that we must endure our dying as our birth; readiness, not choosing the hour, is what matters. Gloucester’s “And that's true too” can be heard as consent, or as a tired man agreeing to keep walking.
evidence: King Lear hath lost, he and his daughter ta'en:
No farther, sir; a man may rot even here.
Men must endure Their going hence, even as their coming hither: Ripeness is all:

questions.prompt: Cordelia wants to face her sisters; Lear answers “No, no, no, no!” What life does he imagine for them in prison? Is it a vision of happiness, or of escape?
facilitatorNotes: They will sing like caged birds, he will kneel to her for forgiveness, they will watch the court’s rises and falls from outside “As if we were God's spies.” It is a picture of love freed from power. But he ignores her wish and the danger: Edmund says only “Take them away.” Readers differ on whether the speech is Lear’s wisdom or a last illusion.
evidence: Shall we not see these daughters and these sisters?
We two alone will sing like birds i' the cage:
When thou dost ask me blessing, I'll kneel down And ask of thee forgiveness:
As if we were God's spies:

readings.title: King Lear — the third sound of the trumpet (V.3)
readings.challenge: Follow Edmund’s fall through the forms of law and knighthood: arrest, challenge, combat, confession.
readings.focus: A secret order, a public combat, and the stories brothers finally tell each other.
readings.context: Recap: The French army has lost; Lear and Cordelia are Edmund’s prisoners, and Lear has told her they will live in prison like birds in a cage. Before the battle a disguised stranger gave Albany Goneril’s letter urging Edmund to kill her husband, and promised to bring a champion if the herald called. King Lear, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Glou. Gloucester, Edm. Edmund, Edg. Edgar, Gon. Goneril, Reg. Regan, Cor. Cordelia, Alb. Albany, Osw. Oswald, Gent. Gentleman, Doct. Doctor, Mess. Messenger, Capt. Captain, Her. Herald). Write happy means call yourself fortunate; retention, custody; impress'd lances, the spears of conscripted men; immediacy, direct authority; compeers, equals; a-squint, cross-eyed; stomach, anger; let-alone, the power to forbid; half-blooded, noble on one side only; attaint, accusation; sub-contracted, promised again; bans, banns of marriage; an interlude, a farce; medicine, here poison; lists, the ground of a combat; canker-bit, eaten by grubs; maugre, despite; fire-new, brand-new; toad-spotted, venomous; say, trace; practice, trickery; cozen'd, cheated; the wheel is Fortune’s; rings, eye sockets; flaw'd, cracked; puissant, strong; tranced, senseless.
readings.contentNote: Edmund gives a secret order to kill; Goneril has poisoned her sister; Edgar tells how his father died.

excerpt.locator: King Lear, Act V, scene III, from Edmund’s order to the captain to Edgar’s naming of Kent; opens “Edm. Come hither, captain; hark. Take thou this note: go follow them to prison: One step…”; closes “…Kent; who in disguise Follow'd his enemy king, and did him service Improper for a slave.”.

questions.prompt: The captain says, “If it be man's work, I'll do't.” What is the work, and what argument has Edmund used to win him?
facilitatorNotes: The written note, we learn later, orders the deaths of Lear and Cordelia. Edmund promises “noble fortunes” and teaches that “men Are as the time is”: tenderness does not suit a soldier. The captain’s grim joke defines man’s work as whatever a horse cannot do; murder becomes a job. The scene sets the clock running on everything that follows.
evidence: men Are as the time is: to be tender-minded Does not become a sword:
I cannot draw a cart, nor eat dried oats; If it be man's work, I'll do't.

questions.prompt: In the quarrel over Edmund, how do Regan and Goneril give themselves away, and how does Albany answer them?
facilitatorNotes: Regan publicly makes Edmund her “lord and master,” giving him her soldiers, prisoners and lands; Goneril mocks her and, aside, reveals that she has poisoned her (“I'll ne'er trust medicine”). Albany arrests Edmund and answers Regan’s claim with dry sarcasm: his wife is already promised, so any suitor must court him. The scene is close to black comedy, as Goneril’s “An interlude!” admits.
evidence: Witness the world, that I create thee here My lord and master.
If not, I'll ne'er trust medicine.
If you will marry, make your loves to me; My lady is bespoke.

questions.prompt: Edgar answers the herald, “my name is lost.” Why does he fight without a name, and what choice does Edmund make that he did not have to?
facilitatorNotes: Edmund’s lies took his name; he must win it back by proving the charge with his sword. By the rules of knighthood Edmund could refuse an unnamed challenger, but pride makes him “disdain and spurn” that safety, and Goneril protests the “practice” too late. The trial by combat assumes that the right will win; the play lets it, this once.
evidence: Know, my name is lost; By treason's tooth bare-gnawn and canker-bit:
What safe and nicely I might well delay By rule of knighthood, I disdain and spurn:
By the law of arms thou wast not bound to answer An unknown opposite;

questions.prompt: Edgar says “The gods are just,” and Edmund answers “The wheel is come full circle.” Do these explanations satisfy you? Weigh them against Edgar’s account of his father’s death.
facilitatorNotes: Edgar sees a pattern of vice punished in kind: Gloucester’s adultery cost him his eyes. Many readers find the justice harsh beyond measure. Edmund’s image is Fortune’s wheel, which turns by chance, not desert. Edgar’s tale then complicates both: he calls his concealment a fault, and his father died when told the truth, his heart bursting “smilingly” between joy and grief.
evidence: The gods are just, and of our pleasant vices Make instruments to plague us:
The wheel is come full circle; I am here.
Never—O fault!—reveal'd myself unto him,
'Twixt two extremes of passion, joy and grief, Burst smilingly.

readings.title: King Lear — “Never, never, never” (V.3)
readings.challenge: Read slowly, marking each moment when hope is raised and taken away.
readings.focus: Deaths reported and seen, a reprieve sent too late, and the last words of a king.
readings.context: Recap: Edgar, at last named, has defeated his brother Edmund in single combat; Edmund has confessed, and Edgar has told how their father died of joy and grief when Edgar revealed himself. Goneril, exposed by her letter, has rushed out; she had poisoned Regan out of jealousy over Edmund. Before the combat Edmund secretly sent a captain with a written order about his prisoners, Lear and Cordelia. Kent, Lear’s counsellor, has served the king in disguise under another name since his banishment. King Lear, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Glou. Gloucester, Edm. Edmund, Edg. Edgar, Gon. Goneril, Reg. Regan, Cor. Cordelia, Alb. Albany, Osw. Oswald, Gent. Gentleman, Doct. Doctor, Mess. Messenger, Capt. Captain, Her. Herald). Fordid and fordone mean destroyed; the promised end is the end of the world; image, likeness; fall and cease, let the heavens fall and all things end; a falchion is a curved sword; crosses, troubles; first of difference and decay, the first change in Lear’s fortune; bootless, useless; boot, reward; poor fool, a term of tenderness; the rack, an instrument of torture; gored, wounded.
readings.contentNote: Cordelia is hanged and Lear carries in her body; Goneril has killed herself after poisoning her sister; Lear dies on stage.

excerpt.locator: King Lear, Act V, scene III, from the bloody knife to the end of the play; opens “Enter a Gentleman, with a bloody knife.”; closes “[Exeunt, with a dead march.”.

questions.prompt: Albany cries “Great thing of us forgot!” What has been forgotten, and what fills the stage while it is?
facilitatorNotes: Lear and Cordelia, under Edmund’s order. The bodies of Goneril and Regan, Edmund’s boast that he “was beloved,” and Albany’s talk of heaven’s judgement take the time that would have saved them. Edmund’s late wish to do “some good... Despite of mine own nature” comes too late. The delay is the play’s cruellest piece of construction.
evidence: Great thing of us forgot!
Yet Edmund was beloved:
some good I mean to do, Despite of mine own nature.

questions.prompt: When Lear enters with Cordelia in his arms, Kent asks, “Is this the promised end?” and Edgar, “Or image of that horror?” What are they comparing the sight to, and why might the play invite the comparison?
facilitatorNotes: To the end of the world, the Last Judgement. The play is set in pagan Britain, but the words reach for the largest horror their hearers know. The father carrying his dead child feels like the end of everything; Lear’s “men of stones” accuses everyone who can still stand dry-eyed.
evidence: Is this the promised end?
Or image of that horror?
Howl, howl, howl, howl! O, you are men of stones:

questions.prompt: Lear tests three times whether Cordelia lives: the looking-glass, the feather, her lips. What does the pattern do, and does he die believing she lives?
facilitatorNotes: Each test raises hope and drops it; between them comes “Never” five times, a line of pure loss. His last words point at her lips, as though he sees breath. Some readers believe he dies in a joyful illusion, as Gloucester’s heart burst between joy and grief; others hear only despair. The text allows both, and the choice changes the ending.
evidence: Lend me a looking-glass;
This feather stirs; she lives.
Never, never, never, never, never!
Look on her, look, her lips, Look there, look there!

questions.prompt: Albany begins to set things right, rewards and punishments, and breaks off at “O, see, see!” Kent refuses to rule. What does the ending say about whether this world can be set right? (This edition gives the last speech to Albany; others give it to Edgar.)
facilitatorNotes: Albany’s speech of justice is cut off by Lear’s grief; Kent will follow his master in death. The final lines refuse formal comfort: “Speak what we feel, not what we ought to say” recalls Cordelia’s honesty in the first scene, where saying what one ought began the disaster. Readers can argue whether the play ends with some order restored or with nothing that answers the loss.
evidence: All friends shall taste The wages of their virtue, and all foes The cup of their deservings. O, see, see!
I have a journey, sir, shortly to go; My master calls me, I must not say no.
Speak what we feel, not what we ought to say.

readings.title: Othello — Iago in the street (I.1)
readings.challenge: Othello is talked about for a whole scene before he appears. Collect what the speakers call him.
readings.focus: A grievance, a secret marriage, and a man who says “I am not what I am.”
readings.context: This run begins Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Rod. Roderigo, Bra. Brabantio, Oth. Othello, Cas. Cassio, Des. Desdemona, Sen. Senator, Off. Officer, Sail. Sailor, Mess. Messenger). Othello is a Moor, a Black African general in the service of the republic of Venice. excerpt.locator: Othello, Act I, scene I, the whole scene; opens “Enter Roderigo and Iago.”; closes “…some special officers of night. On, good Roderigo; I'll deserve your pains. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: What is Iago’s complaint against Othello, as he tells it to Roderigo? How much of it can you trust?
facilitatorNotes: He was passed over for lieutenant in favour of Michael Cassio, a bookish Florentine who “never set a squadron in the field,” though Iago’s worth was proved “At Rhodes, at Cyprus.” Promotion goes “by letter and affection.” The grievance sounds real; but he tells it to a man whose purse he uses, and the sneers (“arithmetician,” “his Moorship’s ancient”) colour it. Readers may disagree about whether this is his true motive.
evidence: Forsooth, a great arithmetician,
Preferment goes by letter and affection,
And I—God bless the mark!—his Moorship's ancient.

questions.prompt: Iago describes two kinds of servant and says which he is. What does “I am not what I am” mean here?
facilitatorNotes: Some servants dote on their “obsequious bondage” and are discarded when old; others keep their “hearts attending on themselves” behind a show of duty, and he is one of those. To wear his heart upon his sleeve would be to give it to the daws. “I am not what I am” makes concealment his very identity: the face he shows is never the self beneath.
evidence: I follow him to serve my turn upon him:
Were I the Moor, I would not be Iago:
I am not what I am.

questions.prompt: How do Iago and Roderigo wake Brabantio? Look at the images Iago uses for the marriage, and why he chooses them.
facilitatorNotes: They shout “thieves!”, putting the daughter among the “bags.” Iago then uses animal images, the black ram and the white ewe, the Barbary horse, the beast with two backs, meant to stir disgust and a father’s fear about grandchildren. He shouts from the dark and lets Roderigo give his name. The racism is Iago’s instrument, and he knows his audience.
evidence: Look to your house, your daughter and your bags!
an old black ram Is tupping your white ewe.
you'll have your daughter covered with a Barbary horse;

questions.prompt: Iago leaves before Brabantio comes down. What reasons does he give, and what do they tell you about how he works?
facilitatorNotes: Venice needs Othello for the Cyprus wars (“Another of his fathom they have none”), so Iago must not be seen against him; he will “show out a flag and sign of love.” He works through others, keeps his own hands clean, and understands the politics better than Roderigo. Brabantio’s “This accident is not unlike my dream” shows a father already half ready to believe.
evidence: It seems not meet, nor wholesome to my place, To be produced
Another of his fathom they have none To lead their business:
I must show out a flag and sign of love, Which is indeed but sign.

readings.title: Othello — “Keep up your bright swords” (I.2–3)
readings.challenge: Compare how Othello and Brabantio behave when the swords are drawn.
readings.focus: Othello’s first appearance, a night of two summonses, and a city at war.
readings.context: Recap: At night in Venice, Iago, who resents Othello for making Michael Cassio his lieutenant, has helped Roderigo, a rejected suitor, wake the senator Brabantio with the news that his daughter Desdemona has eloped with Othello. Iago then slipped away to join Othello at the Sagittary inn, while Brabantio gathered armed men. Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Rod. Roderigo, Bra. Brabantio, Oth. Othello, Cas. Cassio, Des. Desdemona, Sen. Senator, Off. Officer, Sail. Sailor, Mess. Messenger). Yerk’d means stabbed; the magnifico is Brabantio, a grandee; potential means powerful; cable means scope; the signiory is the Venetian government; siege is rank; demerits are merits; unbonneted means as an equal, without doffing his cap; circumscription is restraint; Janus is the two-faced Roman god; a carack is a great merchant ship; attach means arrest; arts inhibited are forbidden practices; composition is consistency; the aim reports means estimates are given; a pageant is a show; brace means readiness for defence; the Ottomites are the Ottoman Turks; Rhodes and Cyprus are Mediterranean islands; engluts means swallows; mountebanks are quacks.
readings.contentNote: Brabantio describes Othello in racist terms and accuses him of witchcraft and of drugging his daughter.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act I, scene II, and scene III to Brabantio’s charge before the Duke; opens “Enter Othello, Iago, and Attendants with torches.”; closes “Bra. Nothing, but this is so.”.

questions.prompt: Iago warns Othello of Brabantio’s power. How does Othello answer, and what does the answer show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He is calm: his services “Shall out-tongue his complaints,” he comes of royal blood though he will not boast of it, and he gave up his “unhoused free condition” only for love of Desdemona. Some readers hear dignity and self-knowledge; others hear a pride that is sure the world will see him as he sees himself. Iago’s claim that he lacks “iniquity” is the scene’s first irony.
evidence: Let him do his spite: My services, which I have done the signiory, Shall out-tongue his complaints.
I fetch my life and being From men of royal siege,
I would not my unhoused free condition Put into circumscription and confine For the sea's worth.

questions.prompt: “Not I; I must be found.” Why does Othello refuse to hide? What is Iago’s oath “By Janus” doing in the same exchange?
facilitatorNotes: Othello trusts that his “parts,” “title” and “perfect soul” will show him as he is: for him appearance and truth agree. Iago swears by a two-faced god. The play will test Othello’s belief that a man is seen rightly, and Iago is the man who is not.
evidence: Not I; I must be found:
My parts, my title and my perfect soul, Shall manifest me rightly.
By Janus, I think no.

questions.prompt: “Keep up your bright swords, for the dew will rust them.” What is the tone of this line, and how does Brabantio’s long speech answer it?
facilitatorNotes: It is commanding, almost amused authority: the fight ends without one. Brabantio answers with law and with the claim that only magic or drugs could explain his daughter running to “the sooty bosom Of such a thing as thou”; prejudice is presented as common sense, “palpable to thinking.” Othello’s reply asks only where he must go to answer.
evidence: Keep up your bright swords, for the dew will rust them.
Run from her guardage to the sooty bosom Of such a thing as thou, to fear, not to delight.
'Tis probable, and palpable to thinking.

questions.prompt: The council opens with confused reports of the Turkish fleet. How do the senators reason their way to the truth, and why show this before Brabantio’s case is heard?
facilitatorNotes: The numbers differ, but every report confirms a fleet; the turn toward Rhodes is judged “a pageant To keep us in false gaze.” They reason from probability and interest, a model for judging Brabantio’s charge, and a warning that shows can be staged to mislead. The Duke’s promise of the law “though our proper son Stood in your action” meets its test when the accused turns out to be the general the state needs.
evidence: 'tis a pageant To keep us in false gaze.
Valiant Othello, we must straight employ you Against the general enemy Ottoman.
yea, though our proper son Stood in your action.

readings.title: Othello — “This only is the witchcraft I have used” (I.3)
readings.challenge: Listen for who gets to tell the story of this marriage, and in what words.
readings.focus: A love story told to the Senate, a daughter’s divided duty, and a father’s warning.
readings.context: Recap: Othello has married Desdemona, the senator Brabantio’s daughter, in secret. Brabantio, roused by Iago and Roderigo, tried to arrest him for bewitching her, but both men were called that night to the Senate, which needs Othello to defend Cyprus against a Turkish fleet. Before the Duke, Brabantio has accused Othello of winning her with spells and drugs. Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Rod. Roderigo, Bra. Brabantio, Oth. Othello, Cas. Cassio, Des. Desdemona, Sen. Senator, Off. Officer, Sail. Sailor, Mess. Messenger). Pith is strength; broil is battle; round means plain; motion is impulse; overt test is open proof; thin habits are flimsy appearances; modern seeming is commonplace likelihood; portance is conduct; antres are caves; the Anthropophagi are man-eaters; dilate means relate in full; intentively means attentively; hint is opportunity; education is upbringing; get means beget; a sentence is a maxim; a grise is a step; agnize means acknowledge; exhibition is allowance; besort is fitting company; quality is nature; a moth of peace is an idler at home; defunct means spent; seel means sew shut, as falconers did a hawk’s eyes; speculative and officed instruments are the eyes and faculties; indign means unworthy; estimation is reputation; delighted means delightful.
readings.contentNote: The Duke’s compliment and Brabantio’s speeches rest on the assumption that blackness is ugly or unnatural.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act I, scene III, from Othello’s defence to his exit with Desdemona; opens “Oth. Most potent, grave, and reverend signiors, My very noble and approved good masters,…”; closes “[Exeunt Othello and Desdemona.”.

questions.prompt: Othello says, “Rude am I in my speech.” Is he? Look at how his defence is built.
facilitatorNotes: The disclaimer is itself rhetoric: a modest frame, then a long, rhythmic tale of “moving accidents,” then the turn to Desdemona’s response, and a closing antithesis that answers the charge of witchcraft. Most readers find him a masterly speaker; some note that he is most fluent when the story is his own life.
evidence: Rude am I in my speech, And little blest with the soft phrase of peace;
I will a round unvarnish'd tale deliver
She loved me for the dangers I had pass'd, And I loved her that she did pity them.

questions.prompt: According to Othello, how did the courtship happen, and who took the first steps? How does that Desdemona compare with her father’s picture of her?
facilitatorNotes: Brabantio invited him; Desdemona listened with “a greedy ear,” wished heaven had made her such a man, and hinted that a friend who could tell his story would win her. She made the first move. Her father’s “maiden never bold,” who would fear to look on Othello, is a daughter he did not know.
evidence: She'ld come again, and with a greedy ear Devour up my discourse:
And that would woo her. Upon this hint I spake:
A maiden never bold; Of spirit so still and quiet that her motion Blush'd at herself;

questions.prompt: How does Desdemona answer “Where most you owe obedience?”, and how does she argue to go to Cyprus? What do her two speeches show about her?
facilitatorNotes: She names “a divided duty” and claims for her husband what her mother gave Brabantio: a precedent from his own marriage that he cannot refuse. Before the Duke she says she loved Othello for his mind (“I saw Othello’s visage in his mind”) and will not be left behind as “a moth of peace,” without “The rites for which I love him.” She is direct, reasoned and open about wanting her marriage; readers often compare Cordelia’s answer about a husband’s share of love.
evidence: I do perceive here a divided duty:
And so much duty as my mother show'd To you, preferring you before her father,
I saw Othello's visage in his mind,
The rites for which I love him are bereft me,

questions.prompt: The Duke tells Brabantio that Othello is “far more fair than black”; Brabantio tells Othello, “She has deceived her father, and may thee.” What do these parting lines assume, and why might they matter later?
facilitatorNotes: The Duke’s praise works by equating black with bad and fair with good: a compliment made of prejudice. Brabantio plants a suspicion that a daughter who deceived could deceive a husband. Othello answers “My life upon her faith!”, and then entrusts his wife to “Honest Iago.” The phrase that should reassure is the one an audience now dreads.
evidence: Your son-in-law is far more fair than black.
Look to her, Moor, if thou hast eyes to see: She has deceived her father, and may thee.
My life upon her faith! Honest Iago,

readings.title: Othello — “Put money in thy purse” (I.3)
readings.challenge: Count how often Iago says “money” and “purse,” and ask whose purse it is.
readings.focus: Iago’s philosophy of the will, and a plan made aloud.
readings.context: Recap: Before the Senate, Othello told how Desdemona came to love him; she defended her choice and asked to go with him to Cyprus, where the Turkish fleet is heading. The Duke agreed and ordered Othello to sail that night, leaving Desdemona to follow in the care of his ensign, Iago, and Brabantio warned that she has deceived her father and may deceive her husband. Roderigo, who hoped to marry her, is left alone with Iago. Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Rod. Roderigo, Bra. Brabantio, Oth. Othello, Cas. Cassio, Des. Desdemona, Sen. Senator, Off. Officer, Sail. Sailor, Mess. Messenger). Incontinently means at once; a guinea-hen is slang for a woman of easy virtue; fond means foolish; hyssop and thyme are herbs; corrigible means correcting; poise means balance; unbitted means unbridled; a sect or scion is a cutting; perdurable means lasting; defeat thy favour means disguise your face; sequestration is separation; coloquintida is a bitter purge; supersubtle means over-refined; conjunctive means joined; traverse is a drill command, march; a snipe is a fool; office here is a husband’s place in bed; plume up means glorify; dispose is manner.
readings.contentNote: Iago speaks of women, sex and Moors with contempt and racist generalisation, and repeats a rumour that his wife slept with Othello.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act I, scene III, from Roderigo’s despair to the end of the act; opens “Rod. Iago!”; closes “…engender'd. Hell and night Must bring this monstrous birth to the world's light. [Exit.”.

questions.prompt: “Our bodies are gardens; to the which our wills are gardeners.” What does Iago believe about human nature? Is any of it a view you could share?
facilitatorNotes: The will governs the self; reason cools “our raging motions”; love is only “a lust of the blood and a permission of the will.” It sounds like self-mastery and responsibility, and many readers find the gardening image persuasive. In his hands it makes love contemptible and everyone else a plant to be managed. Edmund’s scorn for those who blame the stars is a close cousin.
evidence: Virtue! a fig! 'tis in ourselves that we are thus or thus.
Our bodies are gardens; to the which our wills are gardeners:
It is merely a lust of the blood and a permission of the will.

questions.prompt: Why does Iago keep repeating “put money in thy purse”? What is he really saying to Roderigo, and about Othello and Desdemona?
facilitatorNotes: The refrain hammers home one practical instruction, which serves Iago: Roderigo’s money will pass through his hands (“Thus do I ever make my fool my purse”). Around it he predicts the marriage’s failure in racist and misogynist terms (“These Moors are changeable,” “She must change for youth”), offered as worldly wisdom. The repetition also makes the speech comic, and the comedy makes it more dangerous.
evidence: Put money in thy purse; follow thou the wars;
These Moors are changeable in their wills:
Thus do I ever make my fool my purse;

questions.prompt: In the closing soliloquy Iago gives reasons for hating Othello. What are they, and how firmly does he hold them?
facilitatorNotes: “I hate the Moor” comes first, with no reason; then a rumour that Othello has slept with his wife, which he admits he does not know to be true but will act on “as if for surety.” With the lost lieutenancy of the first scene, his motives multiply and shift. Readers have long debated whether they are causes or excuses for a hatred that comes first.
evidence: I hate the Moor;
I know not if't be true; But I for mere suspicion in that kind Will do as if for surety.
To get his place, and to plume up my will In double knavery—

questions.prompt: “The Moor is of a free and open nature, That thinks men honest that but seem to be so.” Why is this compliment the heart of Iago’s plan? Notice the image he chooses as the plan takes shape.
facilitatorNotes: Othello’s virtues, trust and openness, are the weakness Iago will use, as Edmund used his brother’s “foolish honesty.” The plan is born during the speech (“I have ’t. It is engender’d”), and Iago imagines it as a monstrous birth delivered by hell and night: he knows exactly what he is making.
evidence: The Moor is of a free and open nature, That thinks men honest that but seem to be so;
I have 't. It is engender'd. Hell and night Must bring this monstrous birth to the world's light.

readings.title: Othello — the storm and the quay (II.1)
readings.challenge: Watch how each person waits for Othello, and what Iago does with the waiting.
readings.focus: A storm that wrecks an enemy fleet, a wife who lands before her husband, and Iago’s wit.
readings.context: This run begins Act II of Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Mon. Montano, Gent. Gentleman, Cas. Cassio, Des. or Desd. Desdemona, Emil. Emilia, Rod. Roderigo, Oth. Othello, Her. Herald, Clo. Clown, Mus. Musician, Bian. Bianca). Recap: In Venice, Desdemona, a senator’s daughter, has married Othello, a Moor and general of the Venetian army, against her father’s will; the Senate, needing Othello against a Turkish fleet bound for Cyprus, upheld the marriage and sent him to the island, with Desdemona following in the care of his ensign, Iago. Iago hates Othello, who made Michael Cassio his lieutenant over him, and has promised the foolish Roderigo, who wants Desdemona, that he will win her; at the end of Act I he resolved to make Othello believe Cassio too familiar with his wife. A high-wrought flood is a heaving sea; the mortise, the joints of a ship’s timbers; segregation, scattering; the burning bear and the guards of the pole are stars near the Pole Star; enchafed, angry; a Veronesa, a ship from Verona; paragons, surpasses; the ingener, the artist; gutter'd, furrowed; ensteep'd, under water; ancient, ensign or standard-bearer; a se'nnight, a week; birdlime from frize, sticky glue from rough cloth; the cod's head for the salmon's tail, something worthless for something good; small beer, trifles; liberal, free-spoken; gyve, fetter; clyster-pipes, enema tubes.
readings.contentNote: Iago’s rhymes are crude about women and sex, and one plays on “black” and “white” in a play about a Black general.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act II, scene I, from the opening to Othello’s arrival; opens “Enter Montano and two Gentlemen.”; closes “Cas. Lo, where he comes!”.

questions.prompt: The men on the shore cannot see the sea for the storm. How do they describe it, and what has it done?
facilitatorNotes: Waves seem to “pelt the clouds” and throw water on the stars; no ship could hold together. Then the news: the Turkish fleet is wrecked and “our wars are done.” The enemy the play set out to fight is gone in the first scene of Act II, which leaves the danger to come from inside the Venetian camp.
evidence: The chidden billow seems to pelt the clouds;
News, lads! our wars are done.

questions.prompt: Cassio says the seas, “As having sense of beauty,” let Desdemona pass. What do his speeches about her show about him, and how could they be misread?
facilitatorNotes: He idealizes her as “divine,” “our great captain's captain,” and asks the men of Cyprus to kneel to her; he kisses Emilia and explains it as “breeding.” It is courtly worship, the manners of a gentleman. To a watcher looking for desire, every flourish is material.
evidence: As having sense of beauty, do omit Their mortal natures, letting go safely by The divine Desdemona.
She that I spake of, our great captain's captain,
'tis my breeding That gives me this bold show of courtesy.

questions.prompt: Desdemona asks Iago to praise women while she waits. Why does she play the game, and what does his praise of the perfect woman come to?
facilitatorNotes: She is anxious for Othello and says so: “I am not merry,” she is only hiding it. Iago’s rhymes make every kind of woman sexual or foolish, and his ideal woman ends “To suckle fools and chronicle small beer.” Desdemona calls the ending “lame and impotent” and holds her own; Iago, “nothing if not critical,” cannot imagine a woman worth praise.
evidence: I am not merry; but I do beguile The thing I am by seeming otherwise.
For I am nothing if not critical.
To suckle fools and chronicle small beer.
O most lame and impotent conclusion!

questions.prompt: Aside, Iago says, “with as little a web as this will I ensnare as great a fly as Cassio.” What is the web, and what does it tell you about his method?
facilitatorNotes: The web is gesture: Cassio takes Desdemona’s palm, whispers, kisses his own fingers. Iago does not invent the actions; he waits to interpret them. His method is to turn courtesy into evidence by telling the story of it later.
evidence: He takes her by the palm:
with as little a web as this will I ensnare as great a fly as Cassio.

readings.title: Othello — “If it were now to die” (II.1–2)
readings.challenge: Set Othello’s joy beside Iago’s two persuasions: of Roderigo, and of himself.
readings.focus: A happiness so complete it frightens its owner, and a plotter who changes his reasons as he goes.
readings.context: Recap: On the quay at Cyprus, after a storm that wrecked the Turkish fleet, Cassio, Othello’s lieutenant, welcomed Desdemona ashore, and Iago, Othello’s ensign, entertained her with mocking verses about women while they waited; aside he vowed to snare Cassio with the courtesy he showed her. Roderigo, a rich Venetian who wants Desdemona and pays Iago to help him, has come too. Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Mon. Montano, Gent. Gentleman, Cas. Cassio, Des. or Desd. Desdemona, Emil. Emilia, Rod. Roderigo, Oth. Othello, Her. Herald, Clo. Clown, Mus. Musician, Bian. Bianca). Coffers are chests; the master, the ship’s captain; the court of guard, the guardhouse; favour, looks; heave the gorge, retch; pregnant, obvious; conscionable, conscientious; salt, lustful; slipper, slippery; fig's-end and pudding are scornful nonsense; an index, a table of contents; incorporate, bodily; qualification, appeasement; prefer, advance; diet, feed; trash, hold back, as a hound; on the hip, at a disadvantage; rank garb, coarse fashion; mere perdition, utter destruction; offices, the kitchens and storerooms.
readings.contentNote: Iago calls Othello “the devil” whom Desdemona will tire of, and talks of lust in crude terms.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act II, from Othello’s arrival in scene I to the end of scene II; opens “Enter Othello and Attendants.”; closes “…have told eleven. Heaven bless the isle of Cyprus and our noble general Othello! [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: Othello greets Desdemona: “If it were now to die, 'Twere now to be most happy.” Why does his joy make him think of death? How does Desdemona answer?
facilitatorNotes: His content is “so absolute” that nothing in the unknown future could equal it; if happiness has peaked, the rest can only fall. The audience hears a foreboding he does not. Desdemona prays instead that their love will “increase” as their days grow: love as something that goes on, not a summit.
evidence: If it were now to die, 'Twere now to be most happy;
My soul hath her content so absolute That not another comfort like to this Succeeds in unknown fate.
But that our loves and comforts should increase, Even as our days do grow!

questions.prompt: Iago, aside, hears the lovers as music. What does he promise to do to it, and why add “As honest as I am”?
facilitatorNotes: He will loosen the pegs that hold the strings in tune, so the harmony goes flat. “Honest” is the word others use of him and he uses of himself as a private joke; the audience is let into it, which makes us uneasy partners in the plot.
evidence: O, you are well tuned now! But I'll set down the pegs that make this music, As honest as I am.

questions.prompt: How does Iago persuade Roderigo that Desdemona loves Cassio? Separate what he states as fact from what he argues as likely.
facilitatorNotes: He asserts it flatly (“directly in love with him”), then argues from probability: her eye “must be fed,” Othello lacks youth and beauty and is called “the devil,” Cassio has everything Othello lacks. The only evidence is the hand Roderigo saw her take, which Roderigo took for courtesy and Iago renames “Lechery.” The racism of the argument is part of its force with Roderigo.
evidence: Desdemona is directly in love with him.
what delight shall she have to look on the devil?
Yes, that I did; but that was but courtesy.
Lechery, by this hand;

questions.prompt: In his soliloquy Iago gives several reasons for his plot. List them. Does he believe them, and what does the last couplet say about his plan?
facilitatorNotes: He suspects Othello, and Cassio too, with his wife; he says he loves Desdemona partly to feed his revenge; he wants to be “even'd with him, wife for wife,” or failing that to make Othello mad with jealousy. In the middle he admits Othello is “constant, loving, noble.” The reasons multiply rather than convince; many readers find him searching for motives he does not need. The couplet admits the plan is “yet confused” and will take shape only in action.
evidence: Is of a constant, loving, noble nature;
For that I do suspect the lusty Moor Hath leap'd into my seat:
For I fear Cassio with my night-cap too;
'Tis here, but yet confused: Knavery's plain face is never seen till used.

readings.title: Othello — the watch (II.3)
readings.challenge: Track who drinks, who pours, and who stays sober.
readings.focus: Iago arranges a drunken brawl on the first night of peace.

Iago has persuaded Roderigo that Desdemona loves Cassio and set him to provoke Cassio, who commands the watch tonight, into a fight; alone, he has given himself a tangle of reasons for revenge on Othello and Cassio both.
