Desdemona, Emil. Emilia, Rod. Roderigo, Oth. Othello, Her. Herald, Clo. Clown, Mus. Musician, Bian. Bianca). A stop is a restraint; cast, dismissed; a parley, a trumpet call to talks; a stoup, a jug; craftily qualified, secretly watered; innovation, upheaval; pottle-deep, to the bottom of a two-quart pot; a rouse, a full cup; a canakin, a small can; Almain, German; lown, lout; equinox, equal counterpart; the horologe a double set, the clock round twice; ingraft, ingrained; a wicker bottle, a bottle cased in wicker; the mazzard, the head; Diablo, the devil.
readings.contentNote: Drunkenness and a sword fight in which Montano is wounded; Iago’s talk about Desdemona is sexual.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act II, scene III, from the opening to Iago’s “You will be shamed for ever”; opens “Enter Othello, Desdemona, Cassio, and Attendants.”; closes “…ho! The town will rise: God's will, lieutenant, hold; You will be shamed for ever.”.

questions.prompt: Iago tries to get Cassio to talk about Desdemona as a sexual object. How does Cassio answer each suggestion?
facilitatorNotes: Iago calls her “sport for Jove,” “full of game,” her eye a call to provocation; Cassio answers with “exquisite,” “fresh and delicate,” “right modest,” “perfection.” He will not take the bait, though he concedes the eye is “inviting.” The exchange shows Cassio’s decency and Iago testing for a weakness.
evidence: And, I'll warrant her, full of game.
An inviting eye; and yet methinks right modest.
She is indeed perfection.

questions.prompt: Cassio knows he has “very poor and unhappy brains for drinking.” Why does he drink anyway, and what does this show about how Iago works?
facilitatorNotes: Courtesy: the Cyprus gallants want to toast Othello, and Iago presses “but one cup.” Cassio agrees though “it dislikes me.” Iago uses a weakness Cassio has just confessed, and he has prepared the room with Roderigo and three drunken islanders, all on the watch.
evidence: I have very poor and unhappy brains for drinking:
I'll do't; but it dislikes me.
If I can fasten but one cup upon him,

questions.prompt: “I am not drunk now; I can stand well enough.” How does the play make drunkenness comic, and what does Cassio’s drunken theology reveal?
facilitatorNotes: He insists on his sobriety by naming his hands, and decides that in heaven “the lieutenant is to be saved before the ancient.” It is funny, and it is also rank speaking through wine, the very order of precedence that Iago resents. The laughter comes just before the fight.
evidence: the lieutenant is to be saved before the ancient.
this is my right hand, and this is my left.

questions.prompt: After Cassio leaves, Iago tells Montano that drink is Cassio’s nightly habit. Why tell Montano, and why refuse to tell Othello himself?
facilitatorNotes: He builds a false reputation: drink is “evermore the prologue to his sleep.” Montano suggests warning Othello; Iago declines because he loves Cassio, so he appears loyal while others accuse. Then he directs the brawl: Roderigo is sent to “cry a mutiny,” and the bell wakes the town.
evidence: 'Tis evermore the prologue to his sleep:
I do love Cassio well, and would do much To cure him of this evil:
Away, I say; go out, and cry a mutiny.

readings.title: Othello — “never more be officer of mine” (II.3)
readings.challenge: Watch Othello judge the brawl: what he asks, whom he believes, and what he decides.
readings.focus: A general’s judgement, built on the account of the one man who planned the fight.
readings.context: Recap: On the night of celebration in Cyprus, Iago got Cassio, Othello’s lieutenant and commander of the watch, drunk, and set Roderigo to provoke him. Cassio chased Roderigo in, and when Montano, the former governor of the island, tried to stop him, they fought; Montano is wounded. Iago sent Roderigo off to raise the alarm, and the town bell is ringing. Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Mon. Montano, Gent. Gentleman, Cas. Cassio, Des. or Desd. Desdemona, Emil. Emilia, Rod. Roderigo, Oth. Othello, Her. Herald, Clo. Clown, Mus. Musician, Bian. Bianca). The Ottomites are the Ottoman Turks; carve for, indulge; propriety, proper calm; in quarter, at peace; peevish odds, silly quarrel; unlace, undo; censure, judgement; collied, darkened; approved, proved guilty; partially affined, biased by friendship; leagued in office, bound by rank; mince, play down.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act II, scene III, from Othello’s entrance to his exit with Desdemona; opens “Re-enter Othello and Attendants.”; closes “[Exeunt all but Iago and Cassio.”.

questions.prompt: Othello’s first speech asks “Are we turn'd Turks?” What standard is he holding his men to, and what does he fear?
facilitatorNotes: The storm did to the Turks what the Venetians are now doing to themselves; he calls the brawl “barbarous” and appeals to “Christian shame.” He fears for a town still at war and “brimful of fear,” where a bell at night means invasion. It is the speech of a commander first, before a husband.
evidence: Are we turn'd Turks, and to ourselves do that Which heaven hath forbid the Ottomites?
What! in a town of war, Yet wild, the people's hearts brimful of fear,

questions.prompt: “My blood begins my safer guides to rule.” What is happening to Othello as he speaks, and why does it matter?
facilitatorNotes: Anger is darkening his judgement, and he says so; he threatens that whoever caused this will lose him even if they were twins. He keeps control, but this is the first time the play shows his passion pressing on his reason. Iago now knows where to press.
evidence: My blood begins my safer guides to rule, And passion, having my best judgement collied, Assays to lead the way:

questions.prompt: Read Iago’s account of the fight closely. Is anything in it false? How does it hurt Cassio while seeming to defend him?
facilitatorNotes: Most of the facts are true; what is false is the silence about his own part. He says he would rather lose his tongue than harm Cassio, then tells exactly what condemns him, adding that Cassio swore as he never had “till to-night.” “The best sometimes forget” admits the guilt it excuses. Othello thanks him for “mincing” it.
evidence: I had rather have this tongue cut from my mouth Than it should do offence to Michael Cassio;
But men are men; the best sometimes forget:
Thy honesty and love doth mince this matter, Making it light to Cassio.

questions.prompt: “Cassio, I love thee; But never more be officer of mine.” Is the judgement just? Why “I'll make thee an example” when Desdemona appears?
facilitatorNotes: Discipline seems to require it: the officer of the watch caused a riot in a frightened garrison town. But Othello judges without hearing Cassio, who cannot speak, and on Iago’s word alone. Desdemona, woken by the noise, makes the offence personal and public. Readers can defend the sentence as a general’s duty or see it as the first rash act the plot depends on.
evidence: Cassio, I love thee; But never more be officer of mine.
Look, if my gentle love be not raised up! I'll make thee an example.
I pray you, pardon me; I cannot speak.

readings.title: Othello — “Reputation, reputation, reputation!” (II.3)
readings.challenge: Compare what Iago tells Cassio, what he tells himself, and what he tells Roderigo.
readings.focus: Iago’s good advice, and the plan hidden inside it.
readings.context: Recap: Othello broke up the drunken brawl on the watch, heard Iago’s account of it, and dismissed Cassio from his post as lieutenant: “never more be officer of mine.” Iago and Cassio are left alone. Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Mon. Montano, Gent. Gentleman, Cas. Cassio, Des. or Desd. Desdemona, Emil. Emilia, Rod. Roderigo, Oth. Othello, Her. Herald, Clo. Clown, Mus. Musician, Bian. Bianca). Imposition means something put on from outside; cast in his mood, dismissed in anger; speak parrot, babble; fustian, bombast; Hydra, the many-headed monster of Greek myth; denotement, observing; splinter, bind with splints; lay, wager; probal, probable; enfetter'd, chained; function, powers; repeals, calls back; pitch, black tar; fills up the cry, adds to the noise of the pack; cashier'd, dismissed; jump, at the exact moment.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act II, scene III, from Iago and Cassio alone to the end of the act; opens “Iago. What, are you hurt, lieutenant?”; closes “…Soliciting his wife: ay, that's the way; Dull not device by coldness and delay. [Exit.”.

questions.prompt: Cassio cries that he has lost “the immortal part of myself.” What does reputation mean to him, and how does Iago answer?
facilitatorNotes: For Cassio a good name is the soul; without it what is left is “bestial.” Iago calls reputation “an idle and most false imposition,” won and lost without merit, and tells him a bodily wound would make more sense. The advice sounds sensible and comforting. Hold on to it: Iago will say something very different about good name to Othello.
evidence: I have lost the immortal part of myself, and what remains is bestial.
Reputation is an idle and most false imposition; oft got without merit and lost without deserving:

questions.prompt: Cassio says men “put an enemy in their mouths to steal away their brains.” Whom or what does he blame, and is he fair to himself?
facilitatorNotes: He blames wine as a devil, then a second devil, wrath, and ends despising himself. Iago calls him “too severe a moraler.” He did try to refuse the drink; he also drew his sword on a man who tried to stop him. Students can weigh how much is his fault and how much Iago’s.
evidence: O God, that men should put an enemy in their mouths to steal away their brains!
It hath pleased the devil drunkenness to give place to the devil wrath:

questions.prompt: Iago’s advice is to ask Desdemona to plead for him. Why is it good advice, and what makes it dangerous?
facilitatorNotes: It is the natural route: “Our general's wife is now the general,” and she is too kind to refuse. Iago even asks the audience how he can be called a villain for it. The danger is in how her pleading will be presented to Othello: as lust. He says it himself: devils first “suggest... with heavenly shows.”
evidence: Our general's wife is now the general.
she holds it a vice in her goodness not to do more than she is requested:
And what's he then that says I play the villain?

questions.prompt: “So will I turn her virtue into pitch.” How does Iago plan to use each person’s goodness against them? What do his words to Roderigo add?
facilitatorNotes: Cassio’s sincere suit, Desdemona’s kindness and Othello’s love will each become a strand of the net. He calls it “Divinity of hell”: he enjoys the paradox of evil working through good. To Roderigo he preaches patience and wit, “not by witchcraft,” and then fixes the next steps: Emilia will plead for Cassio, and Othello will be brought in at the right moment.
evidence: So will I turn her virtue into pitch; And out of her own goodness make the net That shall enmesh them all.
Divinity of hell!
Thou know'st we work by wit and not by witchcraft,
And bring him jump when he may Cassio find Soliciting his wife:

readings.title: Othello — Cassio’s suit (III.1–3)
readings.challenge: Notice how often people praise Iago’s honesty, and what Iago says at the moment Cassio leaves.
readings.focus: A kind wife keeps her promise to a friend, and the first seed of doubt is sown.
readings.context: This run begins Act III of Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Mon. Montano, Gent. Gentleman, Cas. Cassio, Des. or Desd. Desdemona, Emil. Emilia, Rod. Roderigo, Oth. Othello, Her. Herald, Clo. Clown, Mus. Musician, Bian. Bianca). Recap: Iago got Cassio drunk on watch and drew him into a brawl, and Othello dismissed him as his lieutenant. Iago then advised Cassio to ask Desdemona to plead for him, and resolved in secret to tell Othello that she pleads out of lust for Cassio. The Clown’s jokes are bawdy puns (a “tale” and a “tail”). Quillets are quibbles; a Florentine, a man of Florence, as Cassio is; affinity, family connections; the front, the forelock (a chance seized as it comes); the works, the fortifications; strangeness, coolness; politic, for policy’s sake; supplied, filled by another; watch him tame, keep him awake as a hawk is tamed; a shrift, a confessional; mammering, hesitating; peculiar, personal; poise, weight; wretch, here a word of tenderness.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act III, scenes I and II and the opening of scene III, to Othello’s “Chaos is come again”; opens “Enter Cassio and some Musicians.”; closes “…catch my soul, But I do love thee! and when I love thee not, Chaos is come again.”.

questions.prompt: Cassio calls Iago the kindest and most honest of men, and Desdemona calls him “an honest fellow.” What does the play gain by having so many characters praise him?
facilitatorNotes: Dramatic irony: the audience knows what everyone else does not, and each compliment tightens the trap. “Honest” also meant plain, unpolished, a soldier’s virtue; Iago has made a reputation of it. By now the word is his most effective weapon.
evidence: I never knew A Florentine more kind and honest.
O, that's an honest fellow.

questions.prompt: Desdemona promises: “His bed shall seem a school, his board a shrift.” What does her promise show about her and about her marriage?
facilitatorNotes: She is loyal, energetic and witty; she will keep a friend’s cause “To the last article.” She is confident enough of Othello’s love to tease and pester him. The same persistence is exactly what Iago needs: a wife who pleads too hard for another man.
evidence: If I do vow a friendship, I'll perform it To the last article:
His bed shall seem a school, his board a shrift;
For thy solicitor shall rather die Than give thy cause away.

questions.prompt: Iago says only “Ha! I like not that” and “Nothing, my lord: or if—I know not what.” How can so little do so much?
facilitatorNotes: An unfinished sentence makes Othello finish it himself. Cassio leaves because he feels “ill at ease” in his disgrace; Iago calls it stealing away “guilty-like.” He offers no accusation that could be checked, only a tone.
evidence: Ha! I like not that.
Nothing, my lord: or if—I know not what.
That he would steal away so guilty-like, Seeing you coming.
Madam, not now: I am very ill at ease,

questions.prompt: Desdemona presses for a time: “to-morrow night; or Tuesday morn.” Is she charming, insistent, or both? What does Othello’s last speech reveal?
facilitatorNotes: She teases, counts the days, and says the request is no favour at all; he gives way, “I will deny thee nothing.” Both readings are fair. Left alone he calls her “Excellent wretch” in tenderness and says that if he ever stops loving her “Chaos is come again”: his love is the order of his world, and he has already imagined losing it.
evidence: Why then to-morrow night; or Tuesday morn;
I will deny thee nothing:
Excellent wretch! Perdition catch my soul, But I do love thee! and when I love thee not, Chaos is come again.

readings.title: Othello — the green-eyed monster (III.3)
readings.challenge: Count Iago’s refusals to speak; for each, ask what it makes Othello believe.
readings.focus: Temptation by echo, hint and warning: Iago makes Othello beg for the poison.
readings.context: Recap: Desdemona has promised Cassio to plead for his place and has pressed Othello to receive him; Othello granted it and asked to be left alone. As Cassio left her, Iago murmured “I like not that.” Othello, alone with Iago, has just said that if he ever stops loving Desdemona “Chaos is come again.” Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Mon. Montano, Gent. Gentleman, Cas. Cassio, Des. or Desd. Desdemona, Emil. Emilia, Rod. Roderigo, Oth. Othello, Her. Herald, Clo. Clown, Mus. Musician, Bian. Bianca). A conceit is an idea; close delations, secret accusations; leets and law-days, sittings of local courts; fineless, boundless; exsufflicate and blown, puffed up; secure, overconfident; self-bounty, natural generosity; seel, sew shut, as a falconer did a hawk’s eyes; clime, country; complexion, colouring; in position, in my argument; strain his entertainment, urge his return; haggard, a wild hawk; jesses, the straps on a hawk’s legs; chamberers, gallants; the forked plague, the horns said to grow on a deceived husband; quicken, are born.
readings.contentNote: Iago and then Othello treat Othello’s Blackness and age as reasons a Venetian wife might stray; the racism is Iago’s, and Othello begins to take it into himself.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act III, scene III, from Iago’s “My noble lord” to Othello’s “I'll not believe 't”; opens “Iago. My noble lord,—”; closes “If she be false, O, then heaven mocks itself! I'll not believe 't.”.

questions.prompt: Iago answers with echoes: “Indeed!” “Honest, my lord!” “Think, my lord!” What does Othello notice, and how does he read the hesitation?
facilitatorNotes: He hears the echo as a sign of “some monster” too hideous to show. Because he believes Iago honest, hesitation in such a man must be a secret accusation “working from the heart.” Iago’s reputation turns his silences into evidence.
evidence: By heaven, he echoes me, As if there were some monster in his thought Too hideous to be shown.
For such things in a false disloyal knave Are tricks of custom; but in a man that's just They're close delations,

questions.prompt: “Good name in man and woman... Is the immediate jewel of their souls.” Set this beside what Iago told Cassio about reputation. What does the contrast show?
facilitatorNotes: To Cassio, reputation was “an idle and most false imposition”; to Othello it is the soul’s jewel. Iago’s beliefs change with his listener. The purse lines are ironic too: he has been emptying Roderigo’s purse all along, and he is about to steal a good name.
evidence: Good name in man and woman, dear my lord, Is the immediate jewel of their souls:
Who steals my purse steals trash;

questions.prompt: Why would a man trying to make Othello jealous warn him against jealousy?
facilitatorNotes: Naming the feeling plants it; warning against it makes Iago seem disinterested and wise. His picture of the man “Who dotes, yet doubts” describes the state he is about to produce. The “green-eyed monster” that mocks the meat it feeds on is jealousy devouring the love it lives on.
evidence: O, beware, my lord, of jealousy; It is the green-eyed monster, which doth mock The meat it feeds on:
Who dotes, yet doubts, suspects, yet strongly loves!

questions.prompt: Othello says “she had eyes, and chose me” and “I'll see before I doubt.” How does Iago turn Othello’s own argument against him?
facilitatorNotes: Othello rests on proof and on her free choice. Iago answers that her choice already showed she could deceive: “She did deceive her father, marrying you.” He adds that Venetian wives hide their pranks, “our country disposition,” which the foreign general cannot know. What proved her love now proves her capacity to lie.
evidence: For she had eyes, and chose me.
I'll see before I doubt; when I doubt, prove;
She did deceive her father, marrying you;
I know our country disposition well;

questions.prompt: Alone, Othello says “Haply, for I am black.” Which reasons does he give for losing her, and where did they come from? Does his last line undo them?
facilitatorNotes: His Blackness, his lack of a courtier’s soft talk, his age: Iago has just called her choice of a man not of her own “clime, complexion and degree” unnatural. Othello takes the slur into his own mouth. Then he sees Desdemona and cannot believe it: if she is false, heaven mocks itself. For the moment love still wins; the reasons remain.
evidence: Haply, for I am black And have not those soft parts of conversation That chamberers have,
Not to affect many proposed matches Of her own clime, complexion and degree,
If she be false, O, then heaven mocks itself! I'll not believe 't.

readings.title: Othello — the handkerchief and the vow (III.3)
readings.challenge: Follow the handkerchief from hand to hand, and watch Othello’s demand for proof become a vow without it.
readings.focus: A dropped napkin, a farewell to war, and a sacred vow of revenge.
readings.context: Recap: Iago, pretending reluctance, has led Othello to suspect that Desdemona and Cassio are lovers: by echoing and hinting, by warning him against jealousy, by reminding him that she deceived her father, and by calling her marriage to a Black foreigner unnatural. Alone, Othello began to believe it and then, seeing her, refused to: “I'll not believe 't.” Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Mon. Montano, Gent. Gentleman, Cas. Cassio, Des. or Desd. Desdemona, Emil. Emilia, Rod. Roderigo, Oth. Othello, Her. Herald, Clo. Clown, Mus. Musician, Bian. Bianca). Watching means staying awake; the work ta'en out, the embroidery copied; fantasy, whim; acknown, aware; mandragora, a sleeping drug; owedst, owned; pioners, the lowest soldiers, diggers; quality, rank; circumstance, ceremony; mortal engines, cannon; probation, proof; Dian, Diana, goddess of chastity; topp'd, mounted; bolster, share a pillow; prime and salt, lustful; in pride, in heat; imputation, inference; a foregone conclusion, something already done; aspics, asps, poisonous snakes; fraught, cargo; the Pontic sea is the Black Sea, which flows one way into the Propontic and the Hellespont; capable, all-embracing; clip, surround; remorse, an act of pity.
readings.contentNote: Othello and Iago imagine Desdemona’s supposed adultery in crude sexual and animal images, and swear to kill Cassio and her.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act III, scene III, from Desdemona’s return to the end of the scene; opens “Des. How now, my dear Othello! Your dinner, and the generous islanders By you invited, do…”; closes “Iago. I am your own for ever. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: The handkerchief goes from Othello to the floor to Emilia to Iago. At each step, who knows what? Why does Emilia hand it over?
facilitatorNotes: Othello pushes it away without looking; Desdemona does not see it fall. Emilia knows exactly what it is, “her first remembrance from the Moor,” and that her mistress will “run mad” without it, yet gives it to please a husband who has asked her a hundred times to steal it. Iago snatches it and tells her to forget it. Her divided loyalty is the hinge of the plot.
evidence: This was her first remembrance from the Moor:
I nothing but to please his fantasy.
poor lady, she'll run mad When she shall lack it.

questions.prompt: “Trifles light as air Are to the jealous confirmations strong As proofs of holy writ.” What does Iago understand about jealousy, and is Othello already the man he describes?
facilitatorNotes: Jealousy finds proof in anything; suspicion is a poison that tastes of nothing at first and then burns like sulphur. Othello returns already changed: “Ha! ha! false to me?” The line “I'll not believe 't” lasted only as long as Desdemona was in the room.
evidence: Trifles light as air Are to the jealous confirmations strong As proofs of holy writ:
The Moor already changes with my poison:
Ha! ha! false to me?

questions.prompt: Why does Othello bid farewell to the “plumed troop” and the “big wars” when he believes he has lost Desdemona?
facilitatorNotes: His love and his soldier’s life are bound together: she loved him for his dangers, and his greatness was what he offered her. Without her, war loses its glory and he loses himself: “Othello's occupation's gone!” Some readers hear grand self-pity; others a man whose whole identity is collapsing at once.
evidence: O, now for ever Farewell the tranquil mind! farewell content!
Pride, pomp and circumstance of glorious war!
Farewell! Othello's occupation's gone!

questions.prompt: Othello demands “the ocular proof.” What does Iago give him instead, and why does Othello accept it?
facilitatorNotes: Iago says the sight is impossible and offers “imputation and strong circumstances”: a dream he says Cassio spoke in his sleep, and a lie that he saw Cassio wipe his beard with the handkerchief. Othello, who swore to see before he doubted, calls the dream “a foregone conclusion” and says “Now do I see 'tis true” having seen nothing. Hearing has replaced sight.
evidence: give me the ocular proof;
Nay, this was but his dream.
But this denoted a foregone conclusion:
Now do I see 'tis true.

questions.prompt: The scene ends with both men kneeling. What does each swear, and what does “Now art thou my lieutenant” mean at this moment?
facilitatorNotes: Othello vows a revenge that, like the current of the Black Sea, will never turn back; Iago gives his “wit, hands, heart” to Othello’s service. The kneeling and the heavens called to witness make it a kind of marriage service. Iago gains the post he wanted from the first scene, and his “I am your own for ever” sounds like a lover’s vow.
evidence: Even so my bloody thoughts, with violent pace, Shall ne'er look back, ne'er ebb to humble love,
Now art thou my lieutenant.
I am your own for ever.

readings.title: Othello — “The handkerchief!” (III.4)
readings.challenge: Compare two conversations about a handkerchief: one between husband and wife, one between Cassio and Bianca.
readings.focus: Othello tests Desdemona; she, innocent, answers a different question.
readings.context: Recap: Iago has persuaded Othello that Desdemona is Cassio’s lover, offering a dream he says Cassio spoke in his sleep and a lie that he saw Cassio wipe his beard with the strawberry-spotted handkerchief that was Othello’s first gift to her. Emilia found the handkerchief after Desdemona dropped it and gave it to Iago, who means to leave it in Cassio’s lodging. Othello and Iago have sworn revenge on their knees, and Othello has made Iago his lieutenant. Bianca, who appears at the end, is Cassio’s mistress in Cyprus. Othello, the Moor of Venice, in the Cambridge edition of 1866. Speech prefixes are abbreviated (Mon. Montano, Gent. Gentleman, Cas. Cassio, Des. or Desd. Desdemona, Emil. Emilia, Rod. Roderigo, Oth. Othello, Her. Herald, Clo. Clown, Mus. Musician, Bian. Bianca). Lies means both lodges and tells lies; catechize, question; crusadoes, Portuguese gold coins; humours, moods; a sequester, a separation; castigation, discipline; heraldry, the language of coats of arms; chuck, a pet name; a salt and sorry rheum, a running cold; an Egyptian, a gypsy fortune-teller; a charmer, a sorceress; a sibyl, a prophetess; compasses, yearly rounds; mummy, a drug made from embalmed bodies; startingly, abruptly; advocation, pleading; the blank, the centre of a target; unhatch'd practice, a plot not yet carried out; puddled, muddied; indues, brings; suborn'd, bribed; continuate, uninterrupted; woman'd, with a woman; circumstanced, ruled by circumstance.
readings.contentNote: Othello hints that his wife’s hand shows lust; Emilia speaks bitterly of men who use women as food.

excerpt.locator: Othello, Act III, scene IV, the whole scene; opens “Enter Desdemona, Emilia, and Clown.”; closes “Bian. 'Tis very good; I must be circumstanced. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: Othello takes Desdemona’s hand and calls it moist, hot, liberal, frank. What is he really saying, and what does she hear?
facilitatorNotes: A moist hand was a sign of desire; he prescribes fasting and prayer for the “young and sweating devil” in it, and says that hands are given now without hearts. She hears praise of generosity, answers that the hand gave him her heart, and moves on to her promise about Cassio. They are having two different conversations.
evidence: Hot, hot, and moist: this hand of yours requires A sequester from liberty,
For 'twas that hand that gave away my heart.
But our new heraldry is hands, not hearts.

questions.prompt: Othello tells the history of the handkerchief. What powers does he give it? Does it matter whether the story is true?
facilitatorNotes: A charmer gave it to his mother to keep his father’s love; a prophetess sewed it, the silk was hallowed, the dye made from maidens’ hearts; losing it is “perdition.” The story makes the object stand for fidelity itself, so its loss means the loss of love. Readers differ on whether Othello believes it or tells it to frighten her; either way it works on her, and on him.
evidence: That handkerchief Did an Egyptian to my mother give;
there's magic in the web of it:
To lose't or give't away were such perdition As nothing else could match.

questions.prompt: Desdemona says “It is not lost” and then talks of Cassio. Why does she say it, and why could her timing hardly be worse?
facilitatorNotes: Frightened by the story and his tone, she tells a small untruth and decides he is evading her suit: “a trick.” So she pleads for Cassio at the very moment he demands the token, and the exchange alternates his “The handkerchief!” with her praise of Cassio. To Othello it confirms everything Iago said.
evidence: It is not lost; but what an if it were?
This is a trick to put me from my suit:
I pray, talk me of Cassio.

questions.prompt: Emilia says jealousy is “a monster Begot upon itself.” What does she know that she does not say? How does Desdemona explain Othello’s anger?
facilitatorNotes: Emilia knows where the handkerchief went and keeps silent; her bitterness about men, “all but stomachs,” sounds like her own marriage. Her point is that jealousy needs no cause. Desdemona blames affairs of state and then herself, an “unhandsome warrior” who accused him unfairly. Her generosity to him is touching and, given what the audience knows, painful.
evidence: They are all but stomachs and we all but food;
But jealous souls will not be answer'd so; They are not ever jealous for the cause, But jealous for they are jealous:
I was, unhandsome warrior as I am, Arraigning his unkindness with my soul;

questions.prompt: The scene ends with Cassio giving the handkerchief to Bianca. How does their quarrel echo the main plot?
facilitatorNotes: Bianca, too, reads the token as a sign of another love; Cassio, who found it in his room where Iago planted it, wants the embroidery copied, as Emilia did. He does not want the general to see him with a woman. Jealousy repeats in a lower key, and the handkerchief moves one step closer to where Iago needs it.
evidence: This is some token from a newer friend:
I know not, sweet: I found it in my chamber.
To have him see me woman'd.
